evidence.text: A portable textile with a reported regional origin supports iconographic comparison more securely than a precise travel route.

production.text: Cotton and painted mineral pigments combined textile making with image making.

material-work.text: Weaving supplied a surface and painting supplied imagery. Visible detail and attributed catalogue interpretation do not identify the makers, workshop or rules organizing their labor.

name: A Chavín textile: traveling images?
place: Peru; said to come from the southern coast
geographicPrecision: Broad reported regional origin, not an excavated site coordinate.

interval.label: Fourth–third centuries BCE
interval.note: Current object catalogue dating, reflecting research cited in 2023; not the lifespan of a Chavín state.

question: How might a portable image connect places?
summary: Making this cloth joined two kinds of work: constructing a woven surface and painting an image upon it. Pale crossing threads and red forms remain visible together. The fragment lets us study those choices while keeping its incomplete edges and reported origin in view.

sections.title: A surface was made before an image was painted
sections.text: The catalogue identifies cotton with refined iron-earth pigments. Look first at an unpainted patch: crossing threads make a fabric that could receive an image. Red forms pass over that surface. Weaving and painting offered different ways to shape what a viewer saw. The surviving cloth does not name the people who performed those tasks or show whether one person did both.

citations.locator: Printed p. 8, Fig. 3 and adjacent paragraph

sections.title: A fragment can hold several ways of seeing
sections.text: Follow the red boundaries and compare curving forms with angular ones. The museum reads claws, serpents and paired profile heads, including an inverted head that contributes to a larger fanged image. Changing direction can change what the viewer notices. Its proposed repeating composition extends an interpretation beyond the surviving edges; the missing cloth should remain blank in an annotation.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 8–9, Fig. 3 and adjacent pattern discussion

sections.title: Portable images invite a comparison across places
sections.text: The catalogue relates the imagery to stone carvings at Chavín de Huántar in the northern highlands. Cloth could carry an image in a different way from a fixed carving. This object is said to come from the southern coast, however, so its own itinerary remains unrecorded. Compare materials and motifs before proposing who moved it or who controlled its makers.

returnPrompt: What could turn a proposed movement of imagery into a demonstrated connection?

deeperReading.title: Dating the cloth and the ceremonial centre
deeperReading.text: The Met dates this fragment to the fourth or third century BCE. Archaeologists also date the buildings at Chavín de Huántar, where similar images appear on stone. That chronology helps place the carvings in history, but a shared image cannot tell us when this piece of cotton was woven. The catalogue mentions Burger and colleagues (2023) without a full citation. To check a laboratory date for this particular fragment, we would need a published measurement linked to its museum number, 1987.394.704.

citations.locator: Artwork Details, date and object number. Description paragraph 4 and visible reference list.

deeperReading.title: A weaving guide explains a principle
deeperReading.text: A simple grid can show two sets of threads crossing and distinguish the fabric from a painted mark. Such a modern guide explains a general principle; it cannot supply this fragment’s missing thread counts, loom or original size. Likewise, identifying a repeated image does not identify every wearer, viewer or meaning. A useful annotation directs attention to surviving evidence while leaving those further questions open.

evidenceReading.title: Observe a feature; identify the source of its explanation
evidenceReading.introduction: The photograph, catalogue and reference chronology support different statements. Keep visible features separate from material identification and historical interpretation.

items.label: Threads and red forms
items.text: The existing photograph shows crossing threads, red forms and incomplete edges. The catalogue identifies material and painting.
items.interpretation: A visible colour supports description. Pigment chemistry, fibre identification and a production date need other evidence; no new analysis has been performed.

items.label: An image read at more than one scale
items.text: The museum identifies inverted profile forms contributing to a larger fanged figure and proposes repetition beyond the fragment.
items.interpretation: These are attributed readings of surviving imagery. They do not authorize drawing a complete original cloth or assigning one certain use.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 8–9, Fig. 3 and adjacent pattern discussion

items.label: A comparison is not a route
items.text: Catalogue motif parallels link the inquiry to Chavín de Huántar; the southern-coastal origin is reported.
items.interpretation: A portable material and related imagery make movement a useful question. They do not establish this object’s journey or a state controlling every place where similar images occur.

familyActivity.title: Find a thread; follow a form
steps: Look at the supplied photograph. Point to an unpainted patch where threads cross. Describe it without guessing a thread count.
Find two red forms you think repeat. Follow one boundary with your finger above the screen or print; leave missing areas blank.
An adult can read the caption. Name one observation you can show in the photograph and one explanation supplied by the museum. What remains unknown about where this cloth traveled?
familyActivity.explanation: Crossed threads, visible forms and fragmentary edges are supplied evidence. Material identification, motif interpretation and reported provenance come from the catalogue; the photograph alone supplies no itinerary.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and internal author review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Keep-sized object inquiry with selected institutional reference dates, close observation, a concrete family task and proposed non-destructive photograph callouts. Existing identity, complete case interval, claims, dimensions, object IDs and photograph bytes are preserved.
limitations: Burger et al. 2023 remains unidentified as a consulted technical study. No specimen-matched laboratory number, calibrated date, fibre/pigment result, thread count or loom is introduced. Existing catalogue date wording is retained without claiming an independently verified redating.

Current catalogue says southern-coastal origin is reported. Stronger Ica/findspot wording in the selected Bulletin is not adopted. Complete provenance-tab text, excavation context, original function, individual makers and route remain unavailable or unknown.

The 2004 Met chronology and UNESCO Description/Brief Synthesis use different conventions. Approximate dated reference points do not establish one state, a universal ending or a new architectural sequence. No full excavation report, nomination dossier or source plan consulted.

Only selected Bulletin text was read; PDF-page pixels were not inspectable through the screenshot response. Existing local photograph pixels were inspected. New callouts must retain the original image bytes and distinguish the modern editorial overlay from the ancient object and unknown photography date; missing imagery remains blank.
Independent historian/conservator/community review, family use, screen-reader behavior, physical devices and physical print remain open.

placeStudy.title: A highland centre is not this cloth’s findspot
placeStudy.description: The site point orients the catalogue’s comparison with Chavín de Huántar stone imagery. The original case anchor remains a broad southern-coastal reference for a reported origin; it is not an excavated textile findspot. No line joins the centre to the fragment, and no route, political boundary or place of manufacture is supplied.

points.label: Chavín de Huántar — ceremonial centre
points.text: Rounded UNESCO archaeological-site reference. Buildings, galleries and carved imagery orient a highland centre. Similar imagery does not establish that this cloth was made here or travelled from here to a southern coast findspot.
